title: The number of top-dimensional minimal primes of a Noetherian local ring is bounded by the length of the quotient by a system of parameters
author: The Stacks Project Authors
work: Stacks Project, chapter more-algebra.tex (More on Algebra)
source_version: Stacks Project source tree, file more-algebra.tex, corpus local snapshot 20261012
difficulty_reason: The lemma takes a Noetherian local ring (R, m) of dimension d, lets t be the number of minimal prime ideals of dimension d, and lets (g_1, ..., g_d) be a system of parameters, and asserts t <= length_R(R/(g_1, ..., g_n)) (source lines 38296-38302). The proof reduces to the already established one-dimensional case and then uses Hilbert-polynomial asymptotics. After disposing of d = 0 and reducing d = 1 to the one-dimensional lemma, it assumes d > 1, lists the minimal primes p_1, ..., p_s with the first t of dimension d, and reduces to the case where R is reduced, arguing 'in exactly the same way as in the proof' of the one-dimensional statement (proof lines 38305-38310). For reduced R it forms the exact sequence 0 -> R -> prod_{i=1..t} R/p_i -> Q -> 0 and sets M equal to the product (proof lines 38313-38321). Localizing at p_j shows R_{p_j} -> M_{p_j} = (R/p_j)_{p_j} is surjective, so Q_{p_j} = 0 for all j, hence no height zero prime lies in the support of Q; consequently the numerical polynomial n -> length_R(Q/I^n Q) has degree dim(Supp(Q)) < d (proof lines 38322-38332). The substantive step is the Hilbert-function comparison: by the length additivity lemma — applicable since R does not have finite length — the polynomial n -> length_R(M/I^nM) - length_R(R/I^n) - length_R(Q/I^nQ) has degree less than d (proof lines 38333-38338). Since M is a product of the R/p_i and n -> length_R(R/p_i + I^n) is a numerical polynomial of degree exactly d for i = 1, ..., t, the leading coefficient of n -> length_R(M/I^nM) is at least t/d!; the multiplicity lemma then gives the bound (proof lines 38339-38344). The non-routine content is the support computation for Q together with the leading-coefficient comparison that converts the Hilbert polynomials into the numerical bound.
